utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I address you before the witness enters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we begin with today's testimony, I wanted to say something concerning the motion to have Mr. Krasniqi's statement put into evidence on the 21st of May, and the August statement of 1999. I wanted to move to have that admitted, given that on the 21st of May, 2008, in paragraph 5, he said: "On the 1st of August, 1999, an investigator of the international Tribunal interviewed me in German. It was translated into Albanian but drafted in German. I did not sign it because the investigator didn't ask me to." In the paragraph 6, he says: "I confirm that the number --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Djordjevic kindly repeat the number, and he is reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you've got ahead of the translators, the interpreters, you are reading too quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. [Interpretation] In paragraph 6 he says: "I confirm that the document ERN number K013-6454, K013-6459 is the statement I provide to the investigator of the Tribunal who spoke German on the 1st of August, 1999." In paragraph 7 he says: "I consent to both statements being used in the proceedings against Vlastimir Djordjevic at the ICTY." When we compare the ERN numbers stated in the statements signed by the witness and the ERN numbers from the statement of the 1st of August, 1999, shown to the witness concerning which questions were asked of him, it is clear that it is the same statement. Therefore, I would still seek to tender that that statement be admitted into evidence. Thank you very much, Your Honour. The MFI numbers are D225 and D226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it convenient at this point, Ms. Kravetz, to speak to that motion or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. D'Ascoli was the attorney dealing with this witness, so I'm unable to providing any assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You were passing her the notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I was here, that is true, but I would have to consult with her on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I can address it after the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will deal with it a little later then. Perhaps if the witness is waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Now, I believe Ms. Kravetz has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: My full name is Helge, first name; and Brunborg, last name, spelled B-r-u-n-b-o-r-g.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Dr. Brunborg, what are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I'm trained as an economist and demographer, and I work as a demographer mostly in Statistics Norway currently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Your CV is 65 ter 02503 which is dated November 2003. And the document speaks for itself, so we are not going to go through in detail today in court. But I would just like to ask you if there are any updates that you would like to make to your CV, any current projects that you are involved in that you would like to mention?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't -- remember exactly what the 2003 CV said but since then I've written extensively and also on subjects related to conflict, the area -- demography of armed conflict is something that I've done quite a lot of work on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you told us that you are currently employed in Statistics Norway. What is your position there?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct. My position is -- I'm in -- to be in charge of population projections, and a large survey on -- called generations and gender survey. In addition to doing analyses on Norwegian and international population matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 65 ter of the CV, curriculum vitae, is 02503, and I seek to tender that at this stage. I will not ask further questions on than matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P982, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Dr. Brunborg, I understand that in 2002 you were asked by the Office of the Prosecution to prepare an expert report on the size and ethnic composition of the population in Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, I understand that you have recently reviewed your report in some detail and you've identified some clerical mistakes that you wish to have corrected today in court just to facilitate the reading of the Judges of this report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct. I apologise for the errors, there are many numbers in the report, and all these are -- most of these errors are very obvious, but we should nevertheless correct them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, just to proceed efficiently through these clerical mistakes, what I propose to do is I'll just read the correction that you would like made and just ask you to confirm whether that is correct. Okay? Now, on page 1, paragraph 5, lines 2 and 3 of your report currently read: "... and a de facto population of 2.166 million during the relevant period." I understand that the number given there should be corrected to "2.116 million during the relevant period."

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, on page 2, paragraph 2, line 1, currently reads: "The de facto estimates for 1997 and 1998." And there are two numbers that are give there. I understand that you want this corrected to indicate this -- that the year estimate for 1997, 2.188 million (FSO), and the de facto estimate for 1998, 2.044 million to 2.131 million?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The same page on paragraph 4, line 1, currently reads: "... that the Kosovo population in 1997 was 2.2 million." I understand that the year there in that sentence should be "1995"?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, page 2, paragraph 5, lines 2 and 3, read: "... this figure is very close to the FSO de jure mid-year estimate for 1998 ..." and there's a number given there of "2.220.000," and I understand that this figure should actually be "2.222.000"?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, page 8, footnote 13, the last line of that footnote has a reference to "see table 1," and I understand that that actually should be a reference to "see table 2"?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Page 13 at the bottom, you indicated that the number for -- the estimate for 1998b should actually be 1.378.980?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the final correction, and I understand it's on page 14, paragraph 3, line 3 and 4, which currently read: "This difference is very large, 758.000." And I understand this figure should actually be "750.000."

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Greater than in the previous years. Thank you. So these are all the corrections that you -- clerical mistakes that you wish to correct in your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will get back to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please make breaks between questions and answers, it's very difficult for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: My apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Since we are speaking the same language today, I would just ask you to wait until the cursor stops on the screen before you -- before providing your answer. Your Honours, I'm going to get back to this report later on in my examination, but at this stage I seek to tender it into evidence. It's 01960 is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The report will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P983, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, did you also testify with regard to this report that you prepared for the Office of the Prosecution in the case of Milutinovic et al. in November of 2006?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And before coming to court today, did you have the opportunity to go through the transcript of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Having reviewed your testimony, if today you were asked the same questions that you were asked during your testimony in the Milutinovic case, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I have not become aware of any new information for the period that we are covering in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 65 ter of the Milutinovic transcript is 05334, and I seek to tender that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P984, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, if we could now go back to the main report that you prepared. This is your 2002 report. And if you could just very briefly explain to the Chamber what was the purpose of this report and the mandate that you were given by the Office of the Prosecution when you were asked to prepare it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I was asked by the Office of the Prosecutor to prepare a report on the size of the population of Kosovo and the ethnic composition of this population before the conflict in 1998/1999. So I looked up -- searched for all kinds of relevant information to do that, and I put this information together and wrote this report, assembled the population figures in graphs and tables that -- throughout this report, and wrote a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in summary, what were your conclusions as to the ethnic composition and size of the population in Kosovo during this period?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: During this period the population grew until -- to about 2.1 million before the conflict started. That is in 1998. And of the total population, Albanians constituted about 83 per cent, Serbs about 10 per cent, and others about 7 per cent. That is the main finding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in your report you set out the sources of -- source materials that you used in preparing your report, and these were also discussed during your previous testimony in the Milutinovic case. And you -- in your report you have a section, section 3, which refers to the problems in obtaining population estimates. Could you please elaborate on that and explain to the Judges what were the main problems you had in obtaining population estimates when preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The main problem is a lack of good migration data I would say. Births and deaths are recorded regularly, and there are also censuses every ten years; but lack of good migration data is a problem. Another problem is the difference between de facto and de jure population, de facto is the actual population, the residents in a country; whereas de jure includes those that normally live there or usual residents. And it is not always clear whether the data statistics are given for the de facto or de jure. And censuses may sometimes ask de jure and sometimes de facto populations, so you have to be careful when looking at the results of a census and other population information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were you able to obtain a copy of a census that was up to date in order to be able to prepare your report and estimate the size of the population in Kosovo during the period that you were concerned with?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. I've looked at the information from the Belgrade Institute of Statistics in explaining, defining the terms, census terms, and concepts. And looked at different censuses, including the 1991 census for which there is a very large problem, which I did not mention yet, and that is that the Albanians, Albania population of Kosovo boycotted the census in 1991. So the statistical office in Belgrade estimated the population of Albanians in each village and municipality in 1991 by projecting the population from the -- in 1981 census ten years forwards in time on the basis of assumed rates of births, deaths, and migration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And based on your experience in this field, how reliable are those numbers contained in the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They look pretty reliable because they are quite consistent with other estimates, but of course a headcount would have been more reliable, but I think they did as good job as they could do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, when I was asking you about the main problems you had in obtaining population estimates, you said that the main problem is lack of good migration data. Why does one have to look at migration data when dealing with Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, one reason is that 1991 census was based on estimates and we do not have true or real figures for the migration in between, but there were some -- the Belgrade office made some estimates on that. And after 1991 there's also been -- difficult -- it was a difficult period for Kosovo, and there were flows into and out of Kosovo. And we do not know the -- do not know the exact figures for migration for that period, from 1991 to 1998 especially.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what method did you use to obtain data on outgoing migration from Kosovo in order to prepare your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: First -- I should pause. Sorry. First, I looked at the Statistical Institute of Belgrade estimates of my migration, they have given estimates for each ten-year period prior to 1991. They also made projections for the period after 1991. And secondly, I looked at the survey conducted by several organisations in 1999 and 2000 where they asked for each selected household, whether household members had been absent, some -- or anybody had left, and if they had returned or not. And they asked when they left, and when they returned, if they did. And on that basis, you could estimate the out-migration and, in fact, also in-migration from Kosovo in the previous 12 months, previous 13 months actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you said that you referred to the survey conducted by several organisations. Can you provide more detail as to who conducted these surveys and when they were carried out?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The survey was in charge -- there were French demographers from the University of Bordeaux, and it was funded by UNFPA, United Nations Population Fund. And IOM, which is the International Organization for Migration. And conducted -- the actual interviews were conducted by people from the statistical institutes of Kosovo under supervision of the French demographers and IOM.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you have any information as to how that survey was carried out on the ground?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, they sampled first, the sample areas, municipalities, and then they sampled smaller areas within those; and then they interviewed all household members in all households in a small area. It's a three-stage stamping procedure, as you know. And then they went -- the interviewers went around to all those households and interviewed them on the basis of a questionnaire that had been developed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how were these French demographers able to obtain a representative sample when conducting this survey in order to have reliable data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They drew randomly these samples. I don't recall now exactly the number of areas, but I think there were 30, 40 areas for all of Kosovo; and they drew samples for both urban and rural areas separately. And it is a probability sample where about the approximately 2.5 per cent of the population was covered by these households. So it looks to be comparable or in line with normal standards and sampling theory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. I would like now to look at your report on page 10 both in the English and B/C/S versions. We have a figure 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And it refers to the population of Kosovo by ethnicity and from the -- and covers the period 1948 to 1991. Could you comment on -- do you have that up?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not yet. Now I see the first, page but you said it was page 10. So if it could be moved there, please. Yes, I now see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you please provide your comments on this figure that we have up on the screen, figure 1?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It gives -- it shows two things: It shows the total population which has been growing very fast after 1948, more than doubling. And it also shows the proportion in the three major groups, Albanian, Serbs and others. Albanians have been growing very fast, others also; whereas the proportional and also number of Serbs have been fluctuating more with -- it seems like the highest number was in 1961 and it has -- 1971 actually, and it has declined since then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And during which period do you see the major growth in the Albanian population based on this figure?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Mostly in -- after 1971. After 1961, actually. Throughout the period the growth rate has been almost 3 per cent, which is a high growth rate. 3 per cent per year of the Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now move to figure 2, which is on page 14 of the English and page 15 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is a figure on the total population of Kosovo based on different sources, and I would just ask you again if you could explain to the Judges what is depicted here in this figure.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In this figure I've put together all the information I was able to collect from official, and then unofficial sources. Most of them are de jure figures of the total population from the Federal Statistical Institute in Belgrade. There are also some de facto estimates which are -- or de facto numbers, which are lower. And there are three estimates that sort of stand out compared to the others. One is the Federal Secretariat of Information, estimate for 1998. I think -- okay. I thought that should be for 1995. If I may look at the previous page. Excuse me. No, it is for 1998. The point is that that is much lower than the others, and it is not consistent with this time series. I've looked at this -- at the publication, but I did not find any source of this number where they arrive the data from, method of collecting the data, and there's no explanation. So it is hard to believe that piece of information. And the other -- then there's another estimate for 1995, that was the reason of my confusion, by Islami, which is much higher than the others, although not as much different from the main trend as the previous figure, which seems to be a bit too high, 2.2 million for 1995. Then there is the Blayo et al estimate for 1998 which is bracketed. It's an interval. And that is based on the survey that I just talked about. It is -- an interval is given because its based on a survey, and as we know there are uncertainty in all sample surveys so that's why they have estimated a confidence interval. Finally there is an UNHCR estimate headcount so-called for 1998, which is also consistent with the other figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You mentioned a UNHCR estimate for 1998, could you provide us some information as to how that estimate was carried out?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They needed an estimate of the population. So actually what they did is to project the 1991 population forward from 1991 to 1998. Take both growth rates in the previous ten-year period into consideration but also the proportion of bi-ethnicity in each village. So they did it by village level.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And again based on your experience in the field, how reliable are the numbers provided by UNHCR for this period, based on this projection from the 1991 population census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think it is the best that you could get, and it is pretty reliable. How reliable it is, we will never know. But we should know it is entirely consistent with other estimates both by the statistical office in Belgrade and the Blayo et al estimates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now I would ask you to turn to page 16. This is figure 4. And in the B/C/S this is on page 17. And this is a figure that refers to the proportion of Albanians and Serbs in -- of the Kosovo population. And again I would ask for your comments on the figure that's on that page.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The main feature of it is that we see that very steady increase in the proportion of Albanians from 1951 to 1991. And there we see that the UNHCR estimate for 1998 is very much in line with that trends. On the other hand, we see a steady decline in the number of -- in the proportion of Serbs, especially after 1961. And also the other estimates are consistent with that change, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, earlier you had referred to the estimates from the Federal Secretariat of Information for 1998. And what can you say about those estimates with respect to the proportion of the different ethnic groups in Kosovo according to --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That estimate is much higher than that trend. It is almost 20 per cent, and it does not seem reliable. It looks very unrealistic. But it's difficult to tell how unrealistic it is since I know nothing about the sources and the methodology and -- which has not been explained in the information I have had.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask to make a pause between question and answer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I would ask you to pause before responding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that it's almost 20 per cent higher, I understood, for which ethnic group -- were you referring to a specific ethnic group? Or was this --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I said that the proportion of Serbs is almost 20 per cent according to the Secretariat of Information estimate whereas it is about 10 per cent according to the other estimates. And that does not seem highly likely, especially since there's no explanation why it is so different from the other estimates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, now, I would like to move briefly to the addendum that you prepared in September 2003. If you could just explain what was the purpose of this addendum. And for reference, this is 65 ter 01961.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The OTP requested more information from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the population of Kosovo, and they received that after I finished the main report. So I was asked by OTP to go through this material and comment upon it and perhaps that would warrant a change of conclusion. I did go through the material. There was very little in it that was new. Some of it I knew already. So it did not change my main conclusion as to the size and composition of the population of Kosovo before the conflict started.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is 65 ter 01961, and seek to tender that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P985, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now have 65 ter 00906 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Dr. Brunborg, you are going to have a document appear on the screen before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would ask for page 2 to be displayed in the original for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I would just ask you if ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have page 2. And if we could zoom in a bit for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document before you, Dr. Brunborg?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, this time I saw for the first time yesterday, but it is in any case, preliminary results from the 1991 census; however, I'm familiar with the final results of the census which was published some time after this. This came out in 1992, I believe. So you can say I'm familiar with the numbers of it, although I've not seen this statistical bulletin before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And does this statistical bulletin cover the whole of Serbia for this period, for 1991?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, it does. And with special sections on the autonomous provinces: Vojvodina, and Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at the estimates that are provided for Kosovo province in this document?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And are these numbers consistent with the numbers you saw when you were preparing your report and were looking at the results of the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Certainly. These are the same figures that I refer to in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit -- it's 00906 -- into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P986, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness at this stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz. Mr. Djordjevic, do you cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragoljub Djordjevic, and I'm defending the accused in this case. My colleagues who examined you in the Milutinovic case have already done quite a lot of work, and what I'm going to do today is just try to clear up some things, or rather, I will be asking you some questions, since we are all laypersons here, regarding the task of your -- or rather, the task that you were given by the Prosecution when you were told to draft this expert report. Dr. Brunborg, you received your PhD in economics, and my learned friend Mr. Visnjic asked you about that, but you consider yourself to be a demographer. Could you please tell me, does your PhD have anything to do with the demography since it's in the field of economics or not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, it does, because, first, many of the courses that I took as part of my PhD were in demography, both economics courses and sociology courses. Secondly, the thesis that I prepared, my doctoral thesis, was on the demographic issue. So it's highly related to demography. At that time you could not take a PhD in demography at the University of Michigan, so that's why I took it in economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, today your job is in demography, I assume, and can you please explain this? What is it that you are doing now, today?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I work on Norwegian and international demography at the Statistics Norway in the research division. I'm in charge of population projections for Norway which were published last week, and I do analysis, especially of mortality in Norway, and trends and estimates that affect the population development, and that we need to take account of when we are preparing population projections.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, did you do the same kind of work that you've just described for us at the time when you drafted your expert report, the one that we have here?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, but since then I also have been in charge of a very large survey, sample survey, so I've become more familiar with sample surveys than I used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now that I'm asking you those general questions, you said that you -- well, you say that you deal with demography of war and conflicts. Can you please explain to us what that is, of armed conflicts; and can you explain to us how much that has to do with this report that you produced? Now I'm using the interpretation that I received.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The demography of armed conflict concerns both the consequences of armed conflict for demographic factors, especially mortality, how many people die; but also on migration, displaced persons; and even on marriages and births. That is one side. The other side of the demography of armed conflict is that they are hypotheses that certain demographic factors may cause conflict, and the most -- the fact that is mostly discussed, one is the population pressure, if this high population density in the area then there may be conflict between different groups. Another one is that if the age distribution is skewed, meaning that there are many people, say, young males in certain age groups, say between 18 and 25, then that -- and especially if they are unemployed, then these may cause unrest. So you have both consequences of conflict on demographic factors; and you have the other direction, you have demographic factors that may affect conflict or the risk of conflict. You asked whether this was related to this report, and there's no direct relationship except that I've become more familiar with the literature. I've organised a seminar on this, an international seminar, and edited a book together with colleagues on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, we will agree that this part of your demographic research did not affect your expert report both the first report and the addendum regarding the demography of armed conflict that we talked about?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct. But of course, the more you learn about the field, the more qualified you are to write about it. So indirectly it is useful to know. Although, I would say that in my report I was not concerned with the conflict in Kosovo; I was only concerned with what happened before the conflict and the population development because that was the mandate I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But we will agree again that there's no mention of it in your expert report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will agree with you that the data would have been precious for this court, in this case and in the previous case that has already been completed, that's the Milutinovic case. But in your expert report, you mention that you had limited time for the drafting of the report. In other words, can I then conclude that had you had more time to draft the report, that the report would have been more complete and would perhaps include some other data that might have been relevant for what you put in your basic report? So could you please explain to me what does it mean when you say that you had a limited time to draft the report? When it comes to what you actually wanted to say when you wrote that sentence or phrase.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: By that phrase, I meant that this was done in addition to my regular job in Norway, and I did not have a whole lot of time to spend on it, it was my free time. And I could not spend a lot of time on this. But I do not think that the report would have been very different if I had had more time because I have not come across data sources or literature that would change my conclusions. The report might be longer even, but it might also have been shorter because then I would feel more comfortable with the conclusions if I had spent more time drafting. So basically, I think the report would have been more or less the same. I did also get good be comments from colleagues in several countries which was then strengthening my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You are an eminent person in the scientific circles, and your name is quite well known in our country too and you are held in high esteem as an expert, as a scientist. But could you tell me, is this report a consequence of a direct demand of the Office of the Prosecutor here in The Hague, and what is it that what you wrote in the report, does it reflect the mandate that you received from the Tribunal relating to the basic elements that you are covering in your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, I was asked by the Prosecutor to write a report on the population development in Kosovo. This is what I did. I must admit, I did not really understand why was this issue that needed a special report because already some figures had been published, but I've later learned that there's some debate about this. So they asked me then to go through all available material and draw conclusions on the basis of that. And that is what I have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In fact, my question followed from the response I received to the question that pertained to many other events that might influence demographic movements and changes among other things, what you spoke about in your initial report, you covered it only very briefly when you spoke about migrations, and you spoke about migrations motivated by economic reasons, by political pressure, violence, and other factors. Well, we have a situation where we have an armed conflict within a state, so it's a civil war. You talked about the density of population and so on. So my question to you is this: Was there a different interaction between you and the Office of the Prosecutor, did you propose that such information could be added to the report? And that would have been of great importance for this case.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Within the mandate I was given freehand to write about what I wanted. But the report does not include any causal analysis; it's a purely descriptive presentation of available facts that were not produced by me but by different institutions and people. So I did not try to explain why there was migration, in-migration, out-migration. The only place where I have a few explanatory remarks is on births and deaths where I said that Kosovo was late in the demographic condition, that is, in decline of fertility, and also that -- but that's just a passing remark. There was also no causal analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since we are still on the basic arguments, my next question has to do with the term "demographic transition." It's beginning, duration, and completion, because that's what you are talking about. So could you please clarify this for us because we are laypersons. What would that mean in the case of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The demographic transition is a term that is widely used in demography. It pertains to the transition from a pre-industrial society with high birth and death rates to a modern society with low birth and death rates. In between there is transition. All countries of the world have started this transition, that means all countries of the world have had declining mortality. There are some countries, however, where the fertility or the birth-rate has not started to decline much. That is in -- mostly in Africa. In this regard, what's interesting with regard to Kosovo, is that fertility, or the birth-rate, remained high for a long time in spite of Kosovo having undergone great economic and social development in the post-Second World War period. I think there is a graph on -- showing the birth and death rate. I do not -- let me see. It's on the page 15 in the English version, figure 3, which shows the totality fertility rate or the number of children per women in Serbia excluding Kosovo, and in Kosovo. For Serbia excluding Kosovo it has been around 2 children for women since the mid-1960s, which is on the, you could say the western European level. Whereas for Kosovo, it was very high in 1950s, between seven and eight children. Declined to between four and five around 1980, and has since then declined to between three and four children in 1990. And I have not looked up the data since 1990. But three and a half children is also very high compared to the rest of Serbia and also to other European countries. But it's obvious that also Kosovo is undergoing the demographic transition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that in your report that the transition is drawing to a close in Kosovo, which means that the fertility is no longer at the level it was in the decades that -- in the preceding decades but that it is now coming down to the usual levels, if I may call it that, European levels. Now, what I want to know, as you were drafting your report, the sources that you used, you mention the Federal Institute for Statistics or the Federal Statistical Office, you mentioned your French colleagues, anthropologists from Bordeaux, the whole team, then you mentioned the Federal Secretariat for Information, the UNHCR data, and Islami. From your report, I haven't been able to define whose Islami is, I couldn't even see it from the footnotes.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Are you asking me about Mr. Islami?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I also don't know who he is. His first name is Huizi, and he wrote "Demensioni demografik i ceshjes se Kosoves" published in Pristina in 1997. That is all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But what I want to know is whether you know anything more about him, apart from this study that he did. Do you know if he worked for any organisation in Kosovo, the UNHCR, or anything of the sort? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid not. I did not know anything about him. And this is not published in the Scientific Journal. In sciences we prefer publications, articles that have been published in peer-reviewed journals, so that they are as highly qualified and as objective as possible. There's no -- for other publications, there's no quality stamp, you could say. And this refers both to the Islami study and to the Federal Secretariat of Information, that they may have -- in both cases there may be a hidden agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We will agree that the science you do has often been used for political purposes; but since we are now in a court of law, what we want to know is your scientific knowledge. And my next question that follows up inevitably after your response is whether, in your work using this data, you ever contacted experts from the institutions so that you invoke, so the colleagues who work there in the Federal Statistical Office in Belgrade or somebody from the Federal Secretariat for Information, the UNHCR, the colleagues from Bordeaux; did you personally talk to them? Did you contact them when you did your work perhaps so they might have given you more literature, or more information, or they could have resolved some dilemmas that you may have faced in your work given the data that you had at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I did have contact with the French demographers after I wrote the report, and before my previous testimony to clarify some issues. I did not have time, all the resources to contact, and all the other institutions, unfortunately. That may be -- if you pointed to the fact that I would say that time is limited, and if I had more time and resources, I will of course have contacted these institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As the scientist, you use different methodologies which is obvious from your report. You say that in the area of the former Yugoslavia, the de jure demographic method was used. Was that a method that was common in Europe at the time? You also mentioned a UN recommendation dating back to 1958, to use the de facto method. The method used in the area of the former Yugoslavia, as you said, was the de jure one. Was that the customary method in the various countries of Europe at the time?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, the customary method was the de facto method, because in a census you want to know the size of the population at the given point in time called the census date. And that is why people who are not in the country, especially people who have left and are aware for a long period should not be included. Say tourists are usually included, someone is travelling. But they -- also countries where they only include people who are physically present. There are countries where they introduce a curfew on the census day so they count everybody where they are. People are not allowed to go out. The problem with this method that was applied in the former Yugoslavia was that it often included people who had left the country to work in other -- abroad. Sometimes for long periods, sometimes for many years. So in principle these people could then be included in the census abroad as well and this would not be consistent that people should be counted as living in two different countries at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: From the 1950s onwards, what was the method used in your country, Norway?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was a sort of de facto method. I would say "sort of" because no methods are purely true. Say if somebody is in the hospital or on a short trip then they are also included. However, as of -- from 1970 in my country, we have the Central Population Registry which was then the primary bases for conducting the census. And our last census was in 2001, and we will not have any more regular censuses because all the information from now on will be drawn from administrative registers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your experience monitoring migration because you frequently referred to the data that is missing when Kosovo and Metohija is concerned?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: One way of getting data or information is to ask people in a census whether they have been abroad or been away for a period or somebody else in the household has been away or may still be absent. And if you then ask about the years of migrating, you can estimate migration flows. That is one way. The other way is to ask retrospectively, as in the French survey, if people had been away. But basically the questions are more or less the same. And then you can retrospectively and indirectly estimate migration. A better method would, of course, be if everybody reported when they left the country and when they returned. That is in principle done in my country, although with some weaknesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the system of obtaining permanent or temporary residence in the former Yugoslavia, you said that the method was lacking and inefficient. Why did you not elaborate on that further? Could it be because of the fact that the Albanian population, most of which were Albanians, did not participate in the censuses or perhaps there was no better or proper way of monitoring immigration and migration flows in general? Could you please clarify that in some detail.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question, but let me try to answer. As I said, the Albanian population boycotted the 1991 census, but they participated in previous censuses, although there have been some criticism of the 1971 and 1981 censuses that really not contribute as much as they should or something. But I've not seen any strong evidence on the weaknesses of those censuses. Otherwise, migration is very difficult to measure. Whether it's for Albanians or Serbs or other people. Unless you have a very good system with very good registration of when people leave and when they come back, it is hard. You have to use indirect methods or interview samples or use a census.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question was rather, what was the system like when it comes to recording migration in the former Yugoslavia or in Serbia and Kosovo to be more specific? What could you deduce from the body of law that you have read on that issue? Did you arrive at any conclusions?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Unfortunately I'm not familiar with the law on the former Yugoslavia. There was no -- to my knowledge there was no registration of migration. There was the police, however, had some registers of people and -- but they were not complete. And it was not mostly register. The MUP, the minister of interior, had such a register of people; but I do not think that it was regularly updated with births and migrations. They registered people at a certain point in time, but they had not -- they did not have a good system for revising those registers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since we discussed certain types of analysis, I would now go back to the issue of fertility. Page 3 of your addendum. I think it is the last paragraph or thereabout. Therein you say that between 1981 and 1990 the fertility of the Kosovo population was around 3.000 and that the increase of overall population was some 300.000. I tried to deal -- to do some math here, and it didn't quite tally. The difference of 65.000, you attribute that to the positive migration numbers. That is to say, more people came in than went out. Given that this is a highly unlikely mistake to be made, since I checked that against the English version where net migration is mentioned in that period, perhaps you can explain this to me. In terms of simple math, this is something that I was unable to grasp.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, in the report it says that for the period 1981 to 1990 - and I said perhaps it should be 1991 - according to the source, the population grew, the natural population growth was 433.000; that is the difference between births and deaths. But according to another -- other sources, the difference in population size was 372.000. And then since -- okay, I see. Okay. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [English] That's it.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That was a mistake. Thank you for correcting that. I see your point. It should be a net out-migration, of course. Because the natural population growth was higher than the actual population growth so then you have a loss due to out-migration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now it seems clear to me.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, I would like to add this to the list of misprints, that was -- that was presented earlier today. And I can be specific, if I may. On the page 3 in the addendum, fourth paragraph, second to last line where it says: "Implying that there was net in-migration to Kosovo." It should read: "Implying that there was net out-migration from Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Page 4 of your report relating to the problems of assessing the exact numbers of the population, it is the top paragraph. It says that the most common method is to conduct a census of households. You referred to the data, but when assessment is concerned, or estimate, since I believe it to be a rather problematic issue in terms of your type of research, what would be the basic parameters that you would scientifically use in order to arrive at the level of conclusions of sufficient likelihood and probability that you refer to in your conclusions, which would correspond to the actual basis of the census to be considered accurate? What would be your basis for such conclusions? And perhaps later on we can go into the data you discussed in your report.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you rephrase your questions to be more exact, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You don't have exact data on the census conducted, hence you enter the area of estimates as to how much population there should be of this or that ethnicity, of this or that sex, and everything else that would be included. Which would be the basic elements that you would take into account for the estimates to be as accurate as possible? What would be the components of your estimate? What did the French team do? What was done by the statistics bureau? What was done by the department for information? What was done by the other gentleman you mentioned, Islami? Which would be the parameters that would take you to your conclusion, the basic parameters? That would be my question relating to the method of estimating.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I assume you refer to the 1991 census for Kosovo which the Albanians boycotted. And as I've said already, then the parameters that the Federal Statistical Office in Belgrade used was the -- to get estimates of the population of Albanians in 1991, was to project it from the 1981, so they used 1981 census and their data on births and deaths in the years between 1981 and 1991. Whereas the other source when we wanted to know the population in 1998 before the conflict started, the French demographers, they -- first of all, they had an estimate of the population at approximately that time, but they did not know the -- or at the later time. But they needed to know estimate and migration in the years in between to come up with an estimate. So you could say that counts of population size at one time, and estimates of population changes in between the current time, and the date of the actual estimate were used. Those were the parameters. Please ask if I did not answer your question fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I've completely understood what you said. I wanted to go back to what you answered to my learned friend Mr. Visnjic in Milutinovic et al. He asked you, concerning estimates, he referred to three basic elements: One would be the basic year. The second would be the data on births and deaths. And the third would be data on migration. His question was answered by you positively. You said that one can have positive and negative migration, so out-migration, in-migration, and you basically confirm that these would be the basic elements to arrive at an estimate. Having in mind that answer, as well as some other questions that were put to you, although my question would not be directed at those, my question would rather have to do with the data you had for estimates. You said that the federal statistics bureau is, in your view, realistic in its assessment, then -- as for the information department, you believe their assessment to be unrealistic. As you put your views for all of the researchers involved, the French demographers and Islami as well. What I wanted to ask you is this: As for the UNHCR you said that their estimate is quite close to reality, although the method they used, which, I believe, was based on voters lists, is highly unreliable because it excludes the entire population under the age of 18, since they do not vote. Did you go into assessing the methods used by the various institutions and researchers I enumerated, or was your view of their conclusions based on something else?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course I looked at the methods, but I do not think that UNHCR based its estimate of 2.2 million in 1998 on voters lists. There were voters lists collected later but UNMIK in, I think -- in the year 2000 or 2001. And I agree with you that voters lists are not reliable as a source on the size of a population since it exclude all those who cannot vote under age 18, usually, and all those who did not register to vote. So they can only be used very indirectly, voters lists, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the change of ethnic composition, we can see what the increase rate of the Albanian population as of the 1960s and onwards. All other ethnic communities remained at more or less the same level and the Serb community even decreased in terms of numbers. You mentioned that there's high fertility rate of the Albanian population and a negative fertility rate of the Serb population, I fully agree with that. But in the rest of your report you talk about the volume and cause of the negative -- net out-migration of the Serbs, without mentioning what the cause would be. I wanted to ask you, is it possible that you had no data in terms of references used, or was this caused by something completely different? I would like to hear your explanation of that. There is literally not a single word on the causes of the negative migration trends of the Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: There are two reasons why I did not mention any causes. First, I was not asked to do it; and secondly, that would require a very detailed knowledge about the history and the economic and social situation of Kosovo and Serbs in particular. And it is also a highly political issue that I do not have much knowledge about. So I was asked, as I said, just to review the demographic data. Not to explain the data.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way, as for the immigrants of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, and Serbia proper, from where there were none, you say that these people were of Serb ethnicity. As for those who came from Albania, you did not refer to their ethnic affiliation. Was this an omission on your part, or did you not have any data as to who migrated from Albania to Kosovo? Or did you not know their ethnicity? Or maybe you really didn't have a clue when discussing these types of migration. This is something my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, asked of you in the Milutinovic et al. Case.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Could you please refer to the place in the report where I mentioned these migration flows?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Bear with me. In that case, you even assisted my colleague by pointing out the reference in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic should either read slowly or provide the reference in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Page 7, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In this paragraph I just mention -- refer to migration streams that have been mentioned in the literature; and for many -- most of these migration flows, I do not have any exact numbers. I just mention the flows, where they're from. It says, Migration of Serbs and Albanians from Kosovo from economic reasons, but also violence and persecution; migration into Kosovo from Albania; migration into Kosovo of Serbs from Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, settlement of Serbs, from Central Serbia in Kosovo, et cetera. So I did not mention all the -- what was your question? Why I didn't mention the ethnicity of Albanians from Albania?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No ,no, no, you mentioned in-migration from Albania without specifying what ethnic community moved from where to where. Then you said later that you don't have information on the number of people. My next question -- but you did mention that this was because of the 1992 to 1995 war which was when the Serbs moved in from Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia to Kosovo; that's what you mentioned in Milutinovic at the end of your testimony. And then in response to the question by my learned friend Mr. Lukic, you said the migration of Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina to Kosovo throughout the war of 1992, and 1992 from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you are reading too quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to interrupt, but I would just -- whenever my learned colleague is referring to previous testimony, if we could just have a transcript page reference in order to follow. I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask this to cut a long story short: Do you remember saying that? That's at the very end of your evidence in the Milutinovic case.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Vaguely. I'm familiar with some of the conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia and Krajina, and the refugees flows and that I've read that some of them went to -- went to Kosovo. That is all. This was a -- just examples of migration flows in and out of Kosovo. It was no analyses of the number or the ethnic -- or the ethnicity of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this would be a convenient time for the break so that I can find the exact reference and continue with my cross-examination since we are now one hour and a half into our today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We must have a break now and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 28 of your expert report, you talk about the estimates for the Kosovo Albanians abroad, and here you refer to the estimates made by Mr. Malcolm, and again by estimates by Islami. And they go -- range between 300.000 and 500.000. What can you tell us about the reliability of the data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Excuse me, which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's page 5, in B/C/S. I assume that it's the same page in English. It's the last paragraph. It's in the chapter which is entitled "The Problems in Obtaining Population Estimates," so it's the next page. And it beginning with the sentence: "The FSO estimates of the temporarily absent workers abroad, 28.000 to 91.000 people." And then Malcolm 368.000, and finally Islami, 500.000.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The reliability of the estimates because we can see that the estimates range between 28.000 to half a million Albanians temporarily working abroad. Grecic is also mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I mentioned in the same paragraph, I say that the estimates sited by Malcolm and Grecic include many Albanians who have become residents abroad including many who have emigrated with entire households, leaving nobody to report their absence. So that means they should not be included in the FSO estimates of temporarily absent workers abroad if they have left Kosovo and Serbia and live abroad. That's why you have such widely deferring numbers. Some of these I've left and are not intending to return to live. We don't know about their intentions, but they may have lived abroad for many many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mention Malcolm. Now, I would like you to tell us whether you know what sources he used when he says that in 1993, for instance, 368.000 Kosovo Albanians were living in western European countries?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: To answer that I would need to consult Mr. Malcolm's book, which I do not have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Regarding this information, do you have an estimate as to what data would be closest to the real situation or not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No -- sorry, no, that was not part of my mandate. Of course, if I was asked to do that, I would -- I could go to different countries' censuses, and see if they had a breakdown by nationality, or citizenship, or country of birth, or country of origin, to see how many of the population say in my own country Norway who came from Albania or Kosovo. But even in my country that would be difficult because the country of origin would then be either the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia or later Yugoslavia and later Serbia; and as you know only recently did Kosovo declare dependence, long time after the period we are concerned about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if we'll be able to agree that the estimates are quite arbitrary, the ones that you just mentioned when you actually quote all those authors.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Are you now talking about the number of Albanians abroad or the --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I would need to then check again the sources of Mr. Malcolm and Mr. Grecic who quotes an even higher number, 500.000 Albanians from throughout the former Yugoslavia living abroad. So whether these are inconsistent or unrealistic, I cannot tell you now. But these are -- at least Mr. Malcolm is a recognised author. I don't know about Mr. Grecic. And I think there's been also some debate about Mr. Malcolm's numbers. I've seen a reference to that, but I've not gone into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But I understand that Mr. Grecic made an estimate for the total population of Albanians living all over the world, whereas Mr. Malcolm confined himself to Albanians living in western European countries to the best of my knowledge or understanding.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: You are right. When I re-read that paragraph it say Mr. Grecic talks about Albanians lived -- from throughout the Yugoslavia who lived abroad, and Mr. Malcolm only for those living in western Europe. So that means those figures are consistent. There are, of course, many Albanians who live in countries outside western Europe, say especially United States and Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next paragraph is on the next page. It begins with the word "population estimates" and the first paragraph there you say that several different methods can be used, and the simplest is to extrapolate the growth rate of the population, you've already told us about that. But you say that if this method is used and you don't take into account the age structure dynamics. Could you please explain to us what is age structure dynamics?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The age structure dynamics refers to the population change for each age group. We know that births are only borne by women between approximately 15 and 50 years. Most people die at higher ages, at higher ages also people do not migrate much, so it depends. The number of births and the growth rate depends on the population composition, the age structure of a population. And if you only calculate -- extrapolate growth rate, you do not take this into account. It could be that a population will soon start declining because, although it is growing now, because the fertility rate is low and there are many old people. So that is why. It is more -- it's a better method than just extrapolating growth rates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, the age structure dynamics, as a method, and the growth rate, they are incompatible as methods. And then you go on to say the trends in birth, death, and migration rates. So it's quite clear what this is all about. But the methods to determine the natural growth rate, is that the same thing as the population growth rate or not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It is not. Because the natural growth rate is the difference between the birth-rate and the death rate, whereas the population growth rate also takes the immigration surplus or deficit into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me the method to determine the natural growth rate. Is it mutually exclusive with the population growth rate method, what's the situation there? Because to me as a layperson and to all of us who are not experts in the demography, it would be much clearer if you could tell us that.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: If you take the number of births in a year and divide by the mid-year population, that gives you the birth-rate. You do the same for the death rates: deaths divided by the mid-year population. You subtract these two numbers and then you get the natural growth rate. And you can multiply by 100 to get the per cent, natural growth rate. And again, migrations have not been taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your detailed explanation. The age structure dynamics and the cohort component method, could you please make a correlation there?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The cohort component method is used to project a population by projecting each age group of the population. Say you start in one year and you multiply by the survival rates of that group, and then you'll get the same population one year or five years later that has survived. Then you multiply the number of women in each age group, 15 to 19, et cetera, by the birth-rate for the corresponding age group, and that gives you the population at some future point. But you also would have to take into account migration. If there's no migration, that would be the right figure; but if there's migration, you have to make estimate then. The number of out-migrants by age and the number in-migrants by age. And as we have discussed previously, data on migration are generally much poorer then data on births and deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, as you worked on this report, did you use the data from the provincial statistics bureau from Pristina regarding demographic data or not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I do not think I used many data if at all from Pristina since -- well, at least I did not use for the new office because it was not established at that time before 1999. But there was a provincial office and which assisted in collecting data for the census, and I assume they were also in charge of registering births and deaths which is called the vital statistics system. But all the sources are given as Belgrade, so they transfer the data to Belgrade, the Federal Statistical Office, which then has checked the data, I assume, and produced tables and statistics and books.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, do you know that sometime in late 1950s and early 1960s detailed reports of the provincial office did not end up in Belgrade but they actually remained in Pristina since that time. So as of the 1960s, there are no detailed reports and nothing is centralised in terms of the detailed data. All the detailed data from the -- collected in the census remain in the provincial office.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: But according to the data I've received from Belgrade, they do list data for Kosovo and Metohija, so they must have received the data somehow from Pristina anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: They have the key statistical indicators but the detailed documents are kept in the provincial office, so these documents were not used in the preparation of your report, that's what I wanted to ask you. My next question --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I comment? This was done in all the republics. I'm familiar with the census of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they did the collection of the data and the processing of the tables in Sarajevo and then transmitted, I believe, the tables to Belgrade, not the actual data, what we call microdata or the census forms. And it appears that the same thing was done in Kosovo, in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you will agree with me when I say that the census was taken by the provincial authorities, and not by the federal authority. Each republic in the former Yugoslavia and the provinces in Serbia, they had their own bodies that took the census. Can we agree on that? And the federal government merely put together the forms that were to be used in the course of the census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: My impression is that the federal government did more. They designed the questionnaire, and they gave guide-lines to each republic and, they introduced the law as well. And so they -- there was some supervision of the census in each republic. How close the cooperation was, I do not know. But there was a central committee and a questionnaire that was almost similar in each republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph, or rather, that would be other population estimates in the 1990s, that's what you entitled this chapter, and then the second paragraph, that's page 11 in B/C/S. In English I'm not quite sure, but it's item 7, other population estimates for the 1990s. And it says here that the Albanian population in 1995, the number was 1.96 million. Have you been able to find it? I think it's on page 11 or 12; it's the second paragraph there.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, that is in table 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. But before that, according to the figure in the first column that is provided by Islami, quoted by Grecic in 1999, the Albanian population in 1995 was 1.96 million, which is 89. -- 89.1 per cent of the total population. This figure is not realistic. It's not clear how between 1991 and 1995, the Albanian population could grow so rapidly. 5.1 per cent annually. This growth is much greater than it had been in any previous period. And then you refer to table 3, and you base your on conclusions on this, so that the Albanian population could not experience this growth rate in this period. And when you say that they could not have grown this rapidly by 5.1 per cent per year, do you refer to the natural growth, to the mortality, to migrations, to everything, or to anything specific? So could you please just tell us that. What did you base this on?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: This refers to the total population growth, and I just -- I simply compared the number provided by Mr. Islami and other figures. And 5.1 per cent per year population growth is not possible without migration. You can hardly get above 3, 3 and a half per cent in special circumstances. So there must -- if this is -- these figures are true, it must be due to rather heavy in-migration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it's much clearer. Page 12, again in B/C/S. Paragraph, I believe, four on that page. You say that according to Ms. Blayo, I suppose that she led the team of demographers from Bordeaux, but in 1998 a total population was 2.290.000 people would have lived there had there not been any in-migration, out-migration, and you consider her estimates to be the most reliable. That's what you said at page 2 in the last paragraph. So they are based on a survey carried out after the NATO intervention in Kosovo that between 2.044.000 and 2.131.000 people, you say that Ms. Blayo and her associates estimate that in the period between 1991 and 1998 between 180.000 people and 267.000 people left Kosovo. But you cannot understand how the net out-migration could be greater by 21.000 people in relation to the overall number of population with and without migration. 159.000 people and 246.000 people respectively. So could you please explain this. I mean, you are not clear with this, so could you please tell me what it is that you are not clear? Because I really can't also grasp everything here. I'm not clear myself.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, although there was some inconsistency in the data, and I did not quite understand either. So I remember writing them, Mrs. Blayo and asking about that; I do not recall the answer. I have it with me in my bag; I can look it up. It could be -- the dates are very important here. 1st of October, 1998. The survey was conducted in November, 1998, and it could be that it was in the previous -- referring to 31st of October, and they talk about the 12 month period and also a 13 month period, so this is all confusing. But anyway, I do not think the 21.000 or not is very significant given all the uncertainty about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not everything is clear to me, even after your answer, but I thank you. Nevertheless, I'm not going to dwell on it. When you say that this is not that important. Now, I would like us to go to the literature, the references that you list. Did you use the Federal Statistics Office, the demographic research centre, and the Institute for Social Sciences entitled "The Population and Households in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia" according to the 1991 census published in the 1995 in Belgrade, so did you use that as a source?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Is it in my list of references?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I didn't see it on the list of your references, but this is a source that I consulted since it refers to a critical part of the period that you covered in your report; I believe this to be highly competent, the population and the households in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia according to the 1991 census published in Belgrade 1995.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It looks like I must not have been aware of that publication, but there are other publications that come around at the same time that may have integrated this information. You have publications from the same institute of 1997, 1993, 2001, 1997, 1998. No, not 1998. 1997, statistical yearbooks. So I assume that the information that you refer to was also included in other statistical publications from the statistical institutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to put you my last question in this cross-examination. Your conclusion is that the estimate of the population -- of the Albanian population in Kosovo in 1998 was probably close to 83.6 per cent provided by the UNHCR, almost 84 per cent. You say it is definitely lower than the 89.1 per cent provided by Islami for 1995, and higher than the estimate of the Federal Information Secretariat which had the estimate of 66.5 per cent. You say that there were up to 10 per cent of Serbs maximum, or rather that there were 7 per cent. Even if we take that there were 13 per cent of them, which is not accurate, and if we take the least probable piece of information which is that of the Federal Information Secretariat, was that there was 66.5 per cent Albanians, what is it that would reflect the change of ethnic composition in Kosovo in terms of numbers?
