What numbers would be required to change the ethnic structure in Kosovo if there was say, 66.5 Albanians, 15 per cent of Serbs, and 5 per cent of other ethnicities? What would that mean demographically speaking for the change of the ethnic structure? If you can, of course, provide an explanation.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Sir, I said previously that I did not find the estimate -- that estimate very reliable. And both because it was deviating very much from other results, and also because the sources of the data and the methods were not listed at all. So that's why I think it's completely unrealistic. Now, if trying to be forward to your question, the only thing that could have caused it would of course have been very heavy in-migration flows. So that is the only thing that could cause such a big change in the proportion, and the numbers of Albanians and Serbs. We know that Albanians have higher -- have more births, but in a few years that does not amount to very much. So it is mostly migration that can explain it. Could explain it. But as I said, I do not believe very much in that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This conclude my cross-examination of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Ms. Kravetz, do you re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just very briefly Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, just going back to this last answer you gave, I wanted to clarify your answer. My learned colleague asked you about your conclusions as to the estimates, and you responded that you did not find that estimate very reliable both because it was deviating very much from other results and also because of the source data. Just to clarify, which estimate were you speaking about that you did not find very reliable?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I apologise if I was not so clear, but I was referring to the estimate by the Ministry of the Secretariat of Information for 1998. I think my understanding was that that was what we were talking about. Which was -- let me look to be absolutely clear. Let's see. Excuse me. Federal Secretariat of Information, 1.378 and something, population in 1998. And the ethnic composition according to that a was -- where is, I do not find it right away. Excuse me, perhaps you could help me. The page number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I believe you are referring to the summary of the conclusions of your report, or are you looking for another precise spot?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I was looking for a table, but anyway, that was the figure I referred to. I still say -- I say that the data indicate that the proportion of Albanians in 1998 was 83 per cent, and that the number then of 66 per cent of Albanians is unrealistic, and not reliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Are you referring to figure 4 of your report, or did you have another table in mind?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. Yeah. There's also a table giving you the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to go back to an earlier answer you gave. My learned colleague was asking you - and this is at the bottom of page 30 of today's transcript - as to which would be the basic parameters that you would take into account for your estimates. And you spoke about the 1991 census, and you also referred to the survey done by the French demographers. And I just wanted to clarify your answer with regard to the survey conducted by the French demographers. You said: "... whereas the other source that we wanted to know, the population in 1998 before the conflict started, the French demographers had an estimate of the population at approximately that time, and they wanted to know the migrations in the years in between." And this is at lines 9 to 14 of page 31 of today's transcript? Could you explain what was the -- which estimates did the French demographers have available that you were referring to in that answer when you said "they had an estimate of the population at approximately that time."

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That estimate made by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees as of 31st of March, I believe, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was this the same estimate of the High Commissioner for Refugees that you refer to earlier in your evidence, or was this a different one?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. That's the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, the French demographers relied on the numbers provided by UNHCR and then conducted their survey to be able to estimate the out-going and in-going migration for the period of --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: You are right. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just correct me if it's not a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They also had a later estimate as of August 1999 when the -- which was a headcount, a village headcount which had been made by UNHCR, so that's a second estimate. And -- which resulted in 1.560.000 persons. But that was after the conflict and after lots of migration. So that was the -- that was the other basis, the main basis for the survey. And -- which was then immediately before they started interviewing in November 1999; so I think that is more precise, to refer to that estimate of 1.56 million.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So there are two different UNHCR estimates and French demographers relied on that second one from August 1999?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I apologise for confusing with the previous estimates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, that's okay. It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, those are my questions. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz. You will be pleased to know, Doctor, that concludes the questions for you. We are grateful for your assistance and thank you for troubling to come again to The Hague to help us in this matter, and we wish you well on your journey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the next witness is called, I just wanted to address the matter that was raised by my learned colleague at the start of today's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Having just reviewed the 2008 statement of Mr. Krasniqi, in particular paragraph 6 and 7, we no longer object to the admission of this statement that has been marked for identification as D226, and this is the first August statement with ERN K013-6454/K013-6459.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The number of the second of those statements, do you have -- it's marked as D --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I believe 226 is the one referred to in the witness statement. The 225 is not referred to in this statement. Your Honour, just so we are clear we are withdrawing our objection with regard to the one of them, the one that is not mentioned in the statement; we are maintaining our objection with regard to that, that would be D225.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are maintaining it only with respect to D225?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. Which is the one provided to Dutch police which the witness, I believe, did not recall -- could not provide additional information on yesterday when he testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, anything about that -- the one provided to the Dutch investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not for the time being, but I will address you at an appropriate time when I find it necessary to do at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we'll take as an interim measure that the statement marked for identification as D226 we'll -- marked for identification, will now be received as an exhibit with the same number. Thank you for that. The next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The next witness is Avdyl Mazreku, and he will be led by my colleague Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Now, Ms. Gopalan has some questions for you. Yes, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Are you able to hear me well, sir?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, please --

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, please could you state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Avdyl Mazreku.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And, sir, where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I live in Pastasel village.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Where were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: In Pastasel.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, how old are you now?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I'm now 70 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember giving a statement on the events that took place in your village in 1998 and 1999 to an investigator of this Tribunal? The statement was given in January 2000. Do you remember that statement?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, have you recently had the opportunity to review the statement with the help of a language assistant?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, having reviewed this statement, I understand that you wished to make one substantial correction. I will now read out this correction to you, and you can then confirm for us if you agree with it or not. The correction is at page 4, paragraph 6 of the English; and the B/C/S is page 5, paragraph 4. Sir, you said in that section of your statement: "I could not tell if they were Negroes or just painted faces." Sir, you clarified then in referring to Negroes, you meant tanned persons resembling gypsies or Romas, therefore the correction should read: "I could not tell if they were tanned persons resembling gypsies and Romas, or just painted faces." Sir, do you agree with this correction? Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And, sir, having made this correction to your statement, are you satisfied that the statement is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender 65 ter 05102.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P987, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember giving a second statement to an investigator of this Tribunal in May 2008?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, have you recently had the opportunity to review this statement with the help of a language assistant?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, I had an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, having reviewed the statement, I understand that you wished to make one correction to the statement. I will now read out the correction and if you could please confirm if the correction is correct.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, in page 2, paragraph 8 of your May 2008 statement, the second sentence reads: "These civilians did not include young men below the age of 40 who had fled the village in 1998." Sir, your correction was as follows: You clarified that not all the men below the age of 40 left the village, as some of them remained with their families. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, having made this correction, are you satisfied that this statement is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: What you read to me is true and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender 65 ter 05103, the witness's second statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That too will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P988, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I will now read the witness's in-court summary. The witness is a Kosovo Albanian adult male from Pusto Selo village in Orahovac municipality. The witness will testify that in the autumn of 1998, Serb forces started shelling his village. Consequently, the villagers from Pusto Selo and from surrounding villages fled to the hills. After two days, the Serbian forces surrounded the hills and took the group back to Pusto Selo. There they found a large portion of the village destroyed by fire. The witness will also testify that on the 31st of March, 1999, when Serb forces returned to his village, thousands of villagers, from his own village and surrounding villages tried to flee. The witness saw tanks. The forces that surrounded the villagers ordered the men, including the witness, to separate from women and children. The men were then ordered to empty their pockets. Women and children were searched and sent away. The men were then taken to a stream where they were divided into different groups and then shot at by the Serb forces. The witness was in the fourth and last group. He was injured but survived the shooting with other members from his group. He will testify that on the 31st of March, 1999, 13 men survived the shooting, while 106 men were killed in the village of Pusto Selo that day. That's the end of the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, I now have some questions for you on your statement. As you know, the Judges already have your statements, and so I will just be asking a few clarifying questions. Now, let's start with the incident in September 1998 that took place in your village. This is set out in the English page 2, paragraphs 3 and 4, and the same reference for the B/C/S. Sir, you describe being shelled by Serb tanks, and fleeing to the hills of Kosnik with fellow villagers, and meeting thousands of others from surrounding villages in the hills. You also say: "After two days, the Serbs surrounded us in the hills." Sir, I have some questions for you about the Serbs who you say are police. Sir, what were they wearing, these men who surrounded you in the hills?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: They were wearing police clothes. We were surrounded by policemen, but there were also soldiers elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, when you say police clothes, are you able to tell us what colour these police clothes were?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Are you able to name the colour?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: It was the colour of the sky.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I call up P831, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, shortly there will appear on the screen before you the patterns or the colours of some of the -- of some uniforms. From these patterns before you, are you able to recognise any of them as having been worn or ones that you saw on the men you say were police?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, this one here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, perhaps you could mark the section that you identified.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: The witness has placed a cross on the box on the top left-hand corner of P831.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I would now like to move on to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you wish to tender that?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P989.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, you also say that these men that you saw in 1998 had different patches on their hats and different badges. This is the last sentence of paragraph 4 page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I call up P327, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said. They had red signs on their arms, and they had French hats. We are talking about 1998; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct. We will get to the hats in a moment. But for now, if we could have a look at some of the patches and badges that you talk about. And shortly some of them will appear -- some examples will appear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That's P327, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to see the insignia on the page before you?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Just the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to recognise any of these patches or insignia as the ones you saw in 1998? Perhaps if you have difficulty seeing, you could use your glasses. Yes, please go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Others.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we go to the second page of this exhibit, please. There should be further samples.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, now you see some other examples of insignia. Do you recognise any of these from 1998? If you do, could you just mention the number for us, please.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And is that the only one?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: And number 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Is that the total?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, you also mentioned hats early on in your testimony and in your statement. Again I'd like you to identify, if you can, any hats that you may have seen being worn by these forces in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If we could call up 65 ter 2254 and go to page 13, which is where these sample hats are set out.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, as you can see, there are a number of hats on your screen. Did you see any of these hats being worn by the policemen in 1998?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: There were of this type here, and the French one.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, I'll ask you to place a circle around the hat that you just identified.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And could we go --

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: And I don't see the French hat here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this page into evidence, Your Honours, before I move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1000, Your Honours. I apologise, P990.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now go on to the second page of this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: It should appear on your screen shortly, sir, further examples of hats. Just a moment, sir. Sir, on the screen before you, there are further examples of hats. Could you tell us if you saw any of these in 1999[sic], and if you did, place a circle around the ones you saw.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this page of the exhibit into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P991, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And just as a correction to the transcript. I misspoke when I said "Could you tell us if you saw any of these in 1998," that was an error in my part, I meant "1999" [sic] that's line 6, page 59 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does the witness's answer differ?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I will put the question to him again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, you just placed a circle around a hat that you saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could call up the exhibit, if it's possible. I believe it was P991. No. Okay. I'll try again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The first hat was Exhibit P990.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And my error was in relation to the second hat, which is the exhibit on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P991. Photograph 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Except the marking made by the witness is not on it at the moment, so perhaps I can put the question again and ask him to remark it with Your Honour's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you'll find that the marked one has become the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Which, I believe is P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will take 5 minutes for the system to produce the exhibit, so you could just check with the witness which one he identifies, if any.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Witness, on the screen before you there are a number of hats. Could you tell us if you saw the men in 1998 wearing any of these hats, if at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you mean 1998?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's what the record showed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat your question. It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honours, all my questions so far have related to 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The record reveals 1998. Page 58, line 17. Page 59 line 9 says 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And that was the error, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the error.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For which year are you asking me now?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: You see before you a marking on a hat --

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I already placed a circle.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in which year did you see that hat, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I believe that clarifies the matter, Your Honours. My apologies for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd now like to move on. You say in your statement that these forces "... then took the entire group of us, thousands, back to near the school in Pastasel." This is in paragraph 5 of the English, page 2, same reference as the B/C/S. Sir, if you remember, what did these forces say to you?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: They said that the village had been burned. They said that the terrorists had been there, and for the part that was not burned, they said see here there were no terrorists, and that's why this part has not been burned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And, sir, do you know who burned the village?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Who? The Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Did you see this yourself, sir?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No, when the village was set on fire, we had already fled it. We were hiding.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So how did you know that it was the Serb police that set the village on fire?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Because we found the houses on fire when we returned. They had already been burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to the incident in 1999, and this took place three or four days after the end of Bajram.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And this is set out in the English page 3, paragraph 2; and the B/C/S page 2 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, you describe seeing and hearing a number of tanks at this time. How many tanks did you see?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Seven or eight I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what did these tanks do?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: They had turned their guns towards our population. They stopped about 2-, 300 metres away from us. I actually didn't measure the distance, but I would say that was how far away they were from us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to call up P318, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, as you've mentioned a number of tanks --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, the witness said 1.200 to 1.300 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, as you can see on the screen before you, there are a number of vehicles. Could you tell us if you recognise any of these vehicles as being the ones that you saw in 1999?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, we saw tanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Are any of these vehicles similar to the tanks that you saw on that day?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I don't see any of them here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If we could move on to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The tanks belonged to the army. They had military colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: How about on this page, sir? Are you able to give the number -- could you just read the number out for us, please.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: The number, yes, number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And when you say military colour, what do you mean? What colour are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Green. This is green here, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Moving on, you say: "When the tanks arrived beside us, the men jumped down and surrounded us." Do you remember that happening, sir?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, I do. They surrounded us when they got off the tanks and separated men from women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, what were these men wearing?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: They were wearing green colour clothes, but on the back it was written "policija".

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I didn't count them, of course, but I would say about 30 or 40 of them. Not more than that, when they came to surround us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And once they separated the men from women and children, what did they do?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: When they separated us from women and children, they started to search the women and took away the most valuable things they had, golden jewellery they had. They filled two bags full of them and carried these bags to the tanks. They were big bags.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what happened to the women and children after that?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: After searching them, they ordered them to go in the direction of Ratkovc. And they left. They went in the direction of Ratkovc.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what happened to the men at this stage?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: They kept us males surrounded. After the women and children left, they started to maltreat us, to ask money from us, we gave them some money we had, they wanted more. We gave everything we had on us. We pulled out everything we had in our pockets and through them on the ground, and then they started -- continued their maltreatment of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "they started to maltreat us," are you able to explain what it is they did?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: They beat us up and some -- they beat us, some of us with their weapons butts, and then they started to kick us, and kick blows at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, how many men were there with you in this group?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: In our group there were about 130 men. I think the number must be the one that has already been identified.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, just going back to your statement, you say that: "After the women and children left, it was at this point that many of the group of police also left the area." Now, this is English page 4, paragraph 3. B/C/S page 2, paragraph 4. You also say the police --

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: -- left about 15 of them, separated a group of the youngest men. Sir, can you tell us how old the men in this group were?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, there were some from 14 years of age up to 60 years of age. Some were 40, some were 30. They were younger than us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, early on in your testimony, you made a correction where you said that some young men remained behind in the village to be with their families while many of the other young men had fled the village. Could you tell us why it is that the young men fled your village?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: They fled because they felt insecure. They were afraid of being killed. They killed us elderly people, let alone young people. That's why they left. They would have been shot dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, this group of young men or men that you describe as being a group of the youngest men, could you tell us what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: They were executed before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And where were they executed before you? Could you explain to us how this execution happened?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: They shot them with their automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: When you say "they" who are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: The Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Are you able to describe what they were wearing, please?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Army colour clothes but on their backs was written "policija."

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And after they shot at this group with the automatic rifles, what did the police do next?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: They came back to us, and again demanded money from us telling us that if we didn't give them money, they would kill us. We didn't have any more money left, so they took the second group and executed them like they did with the first group.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how big was the second group?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I would say about 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And, sir, how far away were you from the second group that was executed?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I was about 30, 40 metres away. That was how far the execution place was from us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So what happened to the third group of men?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Again, they came back, again they asked for money, again they maltreated that group; and then they took that group away to the place of execution and again executed them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So when you say "again they came back, again they asked for money," are you referring to the same group of individuals you mentioned earlier, the Serb police?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, the same. Yes, they were the same people. Then they came to our group, which they executed later.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us what happened to your group? How was the execution carried out?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: When they came finally to our group, my uncle, 84 years old, was close to me. He said, I can't stand up, kill me here where I am. And then he turned to me and said, Go back -- and he said, Go back and collect money. Then we held him up by the arms and took him to the execution place. When we went to that bank, I don't know, everything was over.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, how many others were with you in this group, in the group that you were in?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how many of these men survived?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Only 13 of us survived the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: How many of the men in your group survived the massacre, sir?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Only four.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, in your statement you say: "After the killings I heard a Serb voice saying look again, they are moving." And someone else said: "Leave them, they are all dead." This is on page 5, para 5 of the English; B/C/S para 4, page 5. And you also say: "We were lucky it was almost dark." Could you explain what you mean when you say "we were lucky, it was almost dark"?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: It became dark and I heard them say, They are moving still. One of them said, Let them be because they are all dead. It was lucky for us that it became dark and they never returned back to see if any one of us was still alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you've explained to us that a number of different groups were shot at on that day, different groups of men. Could you tell us in total how many men in your village were killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: The total number of men killed are 106. 13 survived. 40 men were from my village.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Some of the survivors had injures on them, some not.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: How about you, what injures did you suffer, if any?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I was hurt on my back.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how long did it take you to recover from this injury?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I underwent an operation because of that, and now I still suffer from my lungs and I have become asthmatic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see that it is time for the break, and I have no further questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a break now before continuing. We will continue at 1.00. So a court officer will assist you during the break, Mr. Mazreku. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think there are now some questions for you from Mr. Djordjevic. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mazreku. My name is Dragoljub Djordjevic, counsel for the accused in this case. I will have some questions for you in order to try and clarify certain facts relevant for this case and its ultimate judgement. Mr. Mazreku, my first question will have to do with examination-in-chief led by my learned friend as well as concerning certain corrections you made in the statements for which you acknowledged as yours and which you had an opportunity to read. You also stated that if you were asked those things today, you would still say the same thing. However, today at the opening of your examination-in-chief, my learned friend before showing you the uniforms, there were four squares with different colours, she also asked you about 1998 and what uniforms were worn by the members of Serb forces. You said that those uniforms were the colour of the sky, that hue of blue, indicating the uniform in the upper left-hand side corner which is a blue camouflage uniform as a matter of fact. As I saw in your statements, as well as what -- from what I could observe in your testimony, I conclude that you can tell the colours. First of all, in your statement of the 15th of January, 2000, you say in paragraph 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps that could be brought up in the Albanian, the 15th of January, 2000 statement. It was admitted as P987 in this case. Can we have the English and the Albanian versions. Page 2 in both. In the Albanian version page 2 as well. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mazreku, look at paragraph 4 on this page, you say: "After two days the Serbs surrounded us in the hills. When I say the Serbs I mean the police, wearing black uniforms. We surrendered to them. Some of them had their faces painted and others did not. They carried automatic rifles and big machine-guns. Some had no markings on the uniforms and most of them as policija or milicija written in Cyrillic on their sleeves. They had red ribbons some were on the shoulder of the uniform. They had different patches on their hats, and many different badges, some with eagles and some with the Serb flag, but most with the four Serbian Cs." Mr. Mazreku, you are obviously referring to 1998 stating that the uniforms were black. We know what black is. And here you said that the uniforms were the colour of the sky. Can you explain to us why did you mention the colour of the sky, that hue of blue, in this context since you have never done that so far in either of the occasions on which you gave statements?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: We, in fact, we don't mean black black, but we mean dark blue. That is what I mean by the word black. Because this is the colour of the police uniform, dark blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me then that when you say that they were the colours of the sky, that you actually had in mind dark blue police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, this is how I said it, I put it. That was the word that came to my mind to describe the colour. I showed you -- I indicated it with my hand. I already showed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mazreku, you are making it much clearer now. In the same paragraph, you say somewhere towards the middle of the paragraph: "Some had no markings on the uniforms and most had either policija or milicija written in Cyrillic on their sleeves." Next --

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then my learned friend showed you certain patches or insignia on the left and the right-hand side asking what were the patches you saw on the uniforms. You indicated two of them, but none of them said policija. On one we could see that it says the Serb volunteers guard, and on the other one there is something else. There is a combination of letters, but neither of them says police or policija. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I said so, and I'm repeating it now, it was written "milicija," it was in different -- it was written on the backs of the police divided in those groups that I mentioned. There were different groups of police, and they had different markings or signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Hold on. Hold on, Mr. Mazreku, we are not discussing 1999; we'll get to that. We are now discussing 1998.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, I'm speaking of 1998 too. In 1999 they were dressed in military colour clothes and on their back was written "milicija".

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It said milicija in 1999 or 1998? Please be precise. Reading your statement one would conclude that that was in 1999.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: In 1999 I saw written "milicija" on their back. The day of the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, I agree.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: 31st of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about 1998 now. The patches you indicated --

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I gave my statement about 1998. I said there were different groups of police, milicija, during the first offensive. They were voluntaries, there were military, there were different groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I know you gave that statement and that is why I'm asking you this. Among the insignia shown to you, there were some written in Cyrillic which said "policija," you did not point those out; you pointed out the Serb volunteers guard patch with some yellow, and the other one was dark blue with a three-letter acronym. On both of these patches, you could see the four Ss or Cs. I'm asking you this: Why did you not indicate those patches which in Cyrillic read "policija"?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I indicated that there were all sorts of signs or patches. There were four or five different groups. Milos, Arkan, Seselj's, they all had their own particular signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any of those bearing the sign of the police in 1998, not 1999?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I saw patches on the sign --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: On the arm. Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Because the regular milicija had it written on their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 there was the regular police and the regular police --

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: -- of 1998. This is what I'm saying, that they had these patches on their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As well as regular police uniforms, is that so?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, with a sign on their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now everything becomes much clearer. Thank you, Mr. Mazreku. My next question for you is this: In 1998 you mentioned the word "offensive" referring to the Serb forces. Who was the offensive directed at? Were there any clashes between the KLA and the police?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No, there weren't clashes, at least not in the place where we were. When the offensive was mounted, there were no clashes. The only thing we heard was that they were saying, We are searching -- we are looking for KLA members, and they fought against the innocent, unarmed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 in the area of your municipality, had there been any KLA presence? Not in your village as such, but in your general area?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I personally never saw any KLA presence. In fact, we were, let's say, wishing to be KLA, but we were not armed, we didn't put up any resistance. We all liked KLA as people. The entire Albanian population were KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I realise that, but I also realise that the KLA existed. I'm not saying that you were a member, I was asking you whether they existed in that area given the fact that you knew of its existence and that you all supported it, I conclude that they did exist.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No, there was no KLA presence. I'm talking of innocent population and not about KLA presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the KLA, not about any civilians. The KLA. You said you were all sympathetic to the causes of the KLA, where did it exist?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: There was no KLA in our village. I don't know if in other parts of Kosovo there was KLA presence. I didn't check that, but in our village there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about the mountains surrounding the villages, was there any KLA there? Were there any operations on their part in Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No, there was no resistance at all in our village. We were people driven out of our own homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you something else. We're still in 1998, were you driven out of your homes, or did you leave on your own because you were afraid and hid in the mountains?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No, they told us that the Serb police are coming and we left because we were afraid to remain at home. That's why we went to the mountains. That is the reason why. Because they set fire to the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The answer is correct, as you said so in your statement, you left your houses of your own accord, scared of the fact that the Serb police was coming. Can you tell us who it was that told you that the Serb police was arriving resulting in you being scared?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Those who saw them. They gave the signal that they were coming, so that's why we left. I don't know the name of the person who said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mazreku, how many inhabitants did your village have at the time?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: About 1.000 inhabitants. 2.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mazreku, was there a person in your village who was the elder of the village, some sort of a leader in the village at the time?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, we had, but even he wouldn't think of his own family interest, let alone of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me the first and last name of the village elder in 1998?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I don't remember now. It's ten years ago. I forgot who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me one other thing: The elected elder of the village, is that person elected for life?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No, he was elected every three or four years. If he worked well, he could stay there for a longer period; if not, they changed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you refer to 1998 mentioning the police, you say that they arrived, adding that there were soldiers at other places as well. You said so at the beginning of your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: May I reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please do so.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: We left in the direction of Koznik mountains, we were surrounded and caught by the Serb police there. Whereas below there around the villages, there was army presence. Personally I didn't see the soldiers, but those who left from that part where the soldiers were told us that there were soldiers there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We've cleared that up. Mr. Mazreku, you were at the foot of Kosnik mountain, that group of refugees comprised several thousand people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, during the first offensive, there were many many people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will point out in particular when we move over to 1999, we are still with the first offensive and 1998. How many people were there in your view, if you can share that with us? That is question number one.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: You mean in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Kosnik mountain. How many of you were there?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I can say we were at least 2.000 to 3.000 people, if not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: To the extent you can recall, can you tell me which villages the people were from who assembled at the foot of mount Kosnik? Were these only the people of your municipality, or were there other people from other municipalities as well?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: People from our municipality came there during the first offensive. They came from Rahovec municipality. There were people from Ratkovc, Radovc, Medja, Doblibar, Pastasel, and other villages. There were people who fled in other directions as well. All I can say is that there were far too many people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said you were surrounded by the police forces, meaning that they finally reached the group of refugees. Once there, did the policemen and their commanders and officers summon heads of villages telling them to take their villagers back to their respective homes and villages?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes. We were sent back. We were told to go to a field in front of the school building. We all gathered there. We were recorded on camera. And then they said to us, You see the village here, this is where the terrorists were. The part where my house was not burned, and they said that there were no terrorists in that part and that's why the houses were not burned. They said that the KLA set the houses on fire. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mazreku. You already said that in your statements. In that field in front of the school, were there only the inhabitants of Pusto Selo who were gathered there, or was it the entire group of refugees of several thousands?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, the entire group of refugees that was caught by them in the mountains was sent back to that field in front of the school, and then in the evening everyone left in their own direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mazreku, did anyone from the police kill any of the civilians on that occasion, the civilians who were there on the slopes of the Kosnik mountain, and later on in the school-yard? Was anyone killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No, they didn't kill any of the civilians, with the exception of some civilians that were taken to the school building where they were beaten and later on arrested. These were young people that were taken by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question, Mr. Mazreku: When the refugees had all gathered on that meadow or lawn, did an ambulance come with the doctors to treat all those who needed medical help, since you say that TV crews were there recording some footage, were they TV cameras or kind of cameras?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: It was a TV camera from Pristina or other agency. They brought some food stuffs there. They distributed some cooking oil and some flour to the people when the people began to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: They brought oil and flour and distributed them to the people, they also brought bread. Was there any bread? Did they also bring bread?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Not everyone got food stuffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to repeat the question, I admit that it is my mistake for not eliciting an answer because I asked two questions and I would like that not to happen yet its happening. Was there an ambulance with a medical team that came there to treat the people who were there?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any ambulance there. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mazreku, could you tell me, did you see the commander who was in charge of this police action as you call it?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No personally I didn't, and I wouldn't have recognised him. I never had any contact with him whoever that might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if your village elder was in charge -- was in contact with the police commander? Of course based on stories or if you have any direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Personally I have no knowledge about this. It is possible, but I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. In the end, Mr. Mazreku, please tell me, you were a citizen of what was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time, the Republic of Serbia, and the autonomous province of Kosovo which is where you lived. Do you know who Vlastimir Djordjevic is?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No, I never saw him. I see him for the first time today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question was not in this context. My question was whether in 1998 you knew who Vlastimir Djordjevic was in the sense of perhaps some state functions or anything that had to do with his job?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No, personally I didn't. I was a citizen of the Yugoslav Republic at the time, but I didn't know who were the ministers, who were the prime minister. I never showed any interest in politics. I am a simple citizen from a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mazreku, now I would like to ask you to tell me what education do you have, and what were you doing before you retired? It's obvious that you had some kind of a job or employment because now you are retired. So where did you work, and what's your educational background?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I've completed eight years of primary school. I worked as a bricklayer. Now I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell me briefly whether you worked in a state-owned company or a private company as a bricklayer?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: I worked for 15 years in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: At home. I had an accident; I became an invalid before I was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mazreku, my next question is whether you spoke at that time, 1998, 1999, Serbian, and whether you are able to read the Cyrillic alphabet without any problems?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to read Serbian. I completed my military service during the time of former Yugoslavia. I do not speak the standard Serbian, but I understand it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell me whether you personally in 1998 -- please tell me whether you personally in 1998 speak to any member of the Serbian forces, either police or the military in 1998?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Had they asked me any question, I would have engaged in conversation with them; by I wasn't asked anything by them, so there was no need for me to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say that they recorded you and you mentioned some agency, some crew from Pristina. Was there just one camera or were there several cameras there? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No, no, it was just one camera, and I think it was a police camera, not a TV camera. Then the Prizren TV channel showed that image to show what allegedly the KLA did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But please tell, me was there the distribution of food, oil, flour, and bread, was this scene also shown?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes. This scene was also shown, to show that they helped us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did you notice any reporter next to this camera, well, apart from the cameraman, a reporter with a microphone in his hand talking to any of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No, this I don't remember. Maybe there was and maybe they talked to someone, but I didn't see it, personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, this will conclude the part that pertains to 1998 with this question. Now, I would like to move on to 1999 to what is extremely unpleasant for you, and I fully understand you in light of the fact that this horrible massacre happened there. Nobody is going to challenge it, nobody can challenge this fact. But what I want to ask you is whether you can tell me -- two days, one day before the massacre, the massacre was on the 31st in the evening; right?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any police presence in your village or not? Or military presence? So any Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No, no, one day before the massacre we were told that the police was coming. We all gathered together, but they didn't come. And then we went back home, and they came the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The next day is the day of the massacre; right?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The 31st of March. They surrounded us at 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will go back to the period that precedes the massacre. You said that you had heard one day before that the police would come, and so you had left and then you had come back because no police had come; but in the day that had preceded that time, was there any police presence or military presence in your village?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me, did people from other villages stay in your village at that time?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Yes. The village was full of them that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for those refugees to have come from other villages to your village and no other village? Did they think that it was safer, or were they guided by some other reasons, if you could tell us?

utterances.speaker: AVDYL MAZREKU
utterances.text: Maybe they thought that it was safer, but nobody was safe at that time. We didn't consider ourselves safe. You couldn't find a safe place. Nobody knew where to hide to for safety reasons. So they wandered from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my assistant has just warned me that our time is up. And I would like to continue my cross-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We must adjourn now for another court takes this courtroom. So we continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. If you could attend then to carry on with your evidence, a court officer will give you assistance when we adjourn. We adjourn until 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th of June, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
